message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Food waste collection feasibility study (Thornbury)

## What the study argues

The study recommends a uniform weekly food waste service across the district from April 2027. It rests on three claims:
- **Participation:** a six-month pilot showed participation held up across houses and flats.
- **Tonnage:** about 3,290 tonnes a year would go to Brookfield, saving £243,000 in incineration costs.
- **Funding:** the net cost of about £490,000 would be fully covered by a £520,000 new-burdens allocation.

The author describes the evidence as strong and the service as fully funded.

The pilot design is good, and the cost arithmetic is correct. But all three claims fail on the document's own figures.

## Errors the document's own figures settle

**1. Participation didn't hold up in flats.**
- Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**, so flats participated at about a third of the rate.
- "Broadly similar across housing types" is contradicted by the table. That statement is repeated in the recommendation and in the author's description.
- The pilot actually suggests flats need a different approach, such as communal bins, collection points or targeted engagement. That approach isn't costed.

**2. The projection uses the wrong participation rate.**
- §3 applies a "64%" rate, but the pilot's overall rate was **57%**.
- 64% appears nowhere in Table 1. The 3,290 tonnes figure does come from 64%: 52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks.
- The pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so its rates can be applied directly. That's a strength of the design.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| As in the study (64%) | 3,290 t |
| Pilot overall rate (57%, 1.9 kg) | 2,930 t |
| Pilot rates by housing type (houses 66% at 1.9 kg, flats 21% at 1.4 kg) | **2,870 t** |

**3. Brookfield can't take the tonnage.**
- Brookfield's capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection is about 1,070 tonnes over that, and the study's own figure is about 1,490 over.
- The saving in §4 assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38. The surplus would have to go to the plant 46 miles away, at an unknown gate fee and with much longer haulage.
- Incinerating the surplus would remove the saving, and probably wouldn't be permitted for separately collected food waste.
- "Treatment is local" is true only for the first 1,800 tonnes.

## What this does to the funding claim

| | Annual cost |
|---|---|
| Gross cost (Table 2) | £733,400 |
| Saving on 1,800 t at Brookfield (× £74) | −£133,200 |
| Saving on ~1,070 t surplus, *best case* (same £74 saving, no extra haulage) | −£79,200 |
| **Net cost, best case** | **≈ £521,000** |

- Even in the best case, the net cost slightly exceeds the £520,000 allocation. Allowing for the surplus going 46 miles at an unknown gate fee, it would be higher.
- The allocation is also only *provisional*: the Government has "indicated" funding.
- "Fully funded" is not supported. What the figures support is a likely funding gap of roughly £0–£100,000 a year, with the exact size open.

## Costs that look incomplete

The Table 2 arithmetic is correct: £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400, and the total is £733,400. But the author's "every cost line is shown" overstates it. Missing or unclear:
- **Relief cover** for sickness and holidays. Six crews with no spares is unusual. It's also unclear whether £34,000 per operative includes on-costs.
- **Supervision and management,** and the dedicated phone line.
- **Liners after the first three months:** the pilot supplied them, and it's unclear whether the service continues to.
- **The approach for flats** (see above).
- **Vehicle purchase:** depreciating the vehicles hides a cash requirement of about £990,000 in 2026–27. The study should say how that will be funded, for example from any capital new-burdens funding.

Separately, fewer residual collections could produce savings that aren't counted. That cuts the other way and is worth estimating.

## Other points

- **Satisfaction.** 81% "of surveyed pilot households" needs a response rate. If respondents were mostly the 57% who participated, the figure overstates satisfaction across all households.
- **Timetable.** A three-to-four-month lead time on specialist vehicles is short by recent standards. Recruiting and training 12 crew in February and March, and delivering caddies to 52,000 households in March, are also tight. There's no contingency if vehicles arrive late. The supplier should confirm delivery in writing.
- **Treatment contract.** Brookfield "has confirmed it can offer" capacity. That is not yet a contract.
- **Statutory deadline.** Under the Simpler Recycling requirements, most English councils had to start weekly food waste collections by 31 March 2026. If Thornbury is starting in April 2027, the study should say whether it's covered by a transitional arrangement. That bears on how urgent the decision is.

## What holds up

- **The pilot design.** It ran for six months, measured weekly by housing type, and used a housing mix matching the district.
- **Participation in houses,** at 66%, and **low contamination** (under 2%).
- **The cost arithmetic** in Table 2, and the £74-per-tonne saving at Brookfield.
- **The implementation plan** works backwards from the vehicle lead time.

## Recommendation

Cabinet shouldn't be told the service is "fully funded" or can be "uniform."

The service is a legal requirement, so the real decision is how to deliver it, not whether. A reasonable course:
1. **Authorise the vehicle order now,** so the timetable isn't lost.
2. **Bring back a corrected study before full approval,** with:
   - tonnage on the pilot's actual rates by housing type;
   - a treatment plan and costs for the tonnage above Brookfield's capacity, including the 46-mile plant's gate fee and haulage;
   - a costed approach for flats;
   - the missing cost lines and the vehicle capital funding;
   - net cost against the allocation, and how any gap would be met if the provisional allocation isn't confirmed or falls short.
